name: PIVCO-Huffman (pivco-huffman)
baseline: huf0 (zstd's Huffman decoder from FiniteStateEntropy, X1 single-symbol and X2 double-symbol variants) and an in-tree traditional 4-stream table Huffman decoder; Oodle Huffman (oo-huff) is wired into bench/bench_fair.c only when an Oodle SDK is linked and does not appear in the BENCHMARKS.md tables
workload: Decode of a 4M-symbol Huffman-coded block sequence repeated 100 times (400M symbols per run), 5 runs, median of 3 best; synthetic distributions (proba80, flat, zipfian, ...) and real files (html_wiki, english, json_api, source_c, ...).
claimed_speedup: Apple M4 Max: proba80 15,339 MB/s vs huf0 X2 2,617 (5.91x best-of-others); real text 4.3-4.8 GB/s, 2.0-2.5x huf0_x2; Xeon 6975P-C AVX-512: english 7,909 vs huf0 X2 1,875 (4.22x), html_wiki 4,765 (2.96x), proba80 22,581 (11.70x). Encoded size within 1-4% of traditional Huffman.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.5.0 on Amazon Linux 2023 for the Xeon 6975P-C (c8i) and Graviton 4 (c8g) tables, clang-20 for the AMD EPYC 7R13 Zen 3 (c6a) table; CMakeLists.txt adds -Wall -Wextra -O3 and, on AVX-512 hosts, -mavx512f -mavx512bw -mavx512vl -mavx512vbmi -mavx512vbmi2 -mavx512vpopcntdq -mavx2 -mbmi2 -msse4.1 -mpopcnt (AVX2 hosts: -mavx2 -mbmi2 -msse4.1 -mpopcnt); Apple M4 compiler not stated
hardware: Apple M4 Max (NEON, block 8192); Intel Xeon 6975P-C AVX-512 VBMI2 (AWS c8i, 2 vCPU); AWS Graviton 4 Neoverse V2 (c8g.large, taskset -c 0); AMD EPYC 7R13 Zen 3 AVX2/SSE4.1 (AWS c6a, 2 vCPU, block 4096)
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in: new bitstream (PivCo partition bitmaps), block-based (4096-8192 symbol blocks), encoder walks the Huffman tree; needs SIMD with permute/compress primitives (NEON, AVX-512 VBMI2, AVX2). Encoded size 1-4% above traditional Huffman. PHA variant adds FSE/ANS coded bitmaps for better ratio on skewed data at lower decode speed.
caveats: README marks the project as WIP and not production-ready; co-authored with an AI assistant per commit trailers. BENCHMARKS.md is a 2026-05-15 snapshot marked 'Last content review: NEVER'. On Zen 3 (SSE/AVX2) html_wiki, json_api and log_apache lose to huf0 X2 at 0.94-0.95x and several rows are only 1.06-1.3x; Graviton 4 real text is 1.29-1.47x. flat_M7 on M4 is only 1.43x. The README TL;DR's real-text range (4.3-4.8 GB/s, 2.0-2.5x) does not include the M4 table's english row (6142 MB/s, 2.55x). In-memory decode-only microbenchmark; huf0 uses 128 KB chunks while PIVCO uses 4096-8192-symbol blocks; tables use the --no-fse (PH) configuration. Paper (PDF on github.io) and arXiv copy not opened (hosts blocked).

name: constriction
baseline: arithmetic coding as implemented in the arcode crate (cgbur/arcode-rs)
workload: Encode and decode of 3-million-symbol i.i.d. messages spanning 0.001 to 10 bits per symbol, from a real-world application, aggregated over all messages.
claimed_speedup: Default ANS (24/32/64): 24.2 ns/symbol encode and 6.1 ns/symbol decode with 0.0015% bit-rate overhead. Default range coder (24/32/64): 16.6 / 14.3 ns/symbol with 0.0237% overhead. arcode arithmetic coding baseline: 43.2 / 85.6 ns/symbol with 0.0004% overhead. About 14x faster decode for ANS and 6x for RC, and 1.8x and 2.6x faster encode (all derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: rustc via 'cargo run --release' (default release profile, no custom RUSTFLAGS in benchmarks/Cargo.toml); rustc version not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7-7500U CPU (2.70 GHz)
tradeoffs: Rust library with Python bindings; no C or C++ API, so use from C++ needs an FFI wrapper. ANS is last-in-first-out (suits bits-back coding), RC is first-in-first-out. Models are user-supplied (probability tables), so this measures the coder core, not a full compressor. Small-precision presets trade 4% bit-rate overhead for speed.
caveats: First-party benchmark from the author's arXiv preprint (arXiv:2201.01741, Section 5.2), not peer-reviewed. The benchmark code (bamler-lab/understanding-ans/benchmarks, 10 timed runs per message with cool-down pauses) is public but pins constriction 0.1.4 and arcode 0.2.3, so the README numbers describe an old library version. rustc version not stated. Baseline is a Rust arithmetic coder (arcode crate), not Huffman, rANS or Huff0, and nothing in C or C++; not compared against FSE, Huff0 or ryg_rans. The arcode coder has a slightly lower bit-rate overhead (0.0004% versus 0.0015% for default ANS).

name: FPC (Fast Prefix Coder)
baseline: zlib Huffman (zlibh) and FSE Huff0 (fsehuf) as packaged in TurboBench
workload: Order-0 entropy coding of silesia.tar (211 MB) on a Core i5-4460 and of enwik8 on an Orange Pi PC Plus (Allwinner H3), run through TurboBench.
claimed_speedup: silesia.tar (Core i5-4460, TurboBench): fpc 32 decodes at 897.28 MB/s versus 715.36 MB/s for fsehuf, 591.30 MB/s for rans_static16, 483.55 MB/s for fse and 243.08 MB/s for zlibh (about 1.25x fsehuf and 3.7x zlibh, derived from page data); fpc 16 compresses at 476.96 MB/s versus 248.55 MB/s for zlibh and decodes at 821.30 MB/s. Ratios are within 0.1 percentage points (61.4% for fpc 32 and fsehuf). On the Allwinner H3 board, enwik8: fpc 32 decodes at 90.70 MB/s versus 61.11 MB/s for fsehuf and 62.90 MB/s for zlibh. Independent powturbo Entropy Coder Benchmark (snippet only, file and CPU not seen): FPC 32 decode 928.53 MB/s versus FSEhuf 32 at 831.45 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark run; the standalone Makefile uses -Wall -O2 -std=c99 -DNDEBUG
hardware: Intel Core i5-4460 @ 3.20GHz (silesia.tar); Orange Pi PC Plus, Allwinner H3 (enwik8)
tradeoffs: Prefix (Huffman) coder with length-limited package-merge codes (default max 11 bits), 3 interleaved streams by default, adaptive block subdivision. Static per block, so it cannot reach the ratio of adaptive arithmetic coders such as fpaq0p_sh (58.7% on silesia.tar).
caveats: The README tables were run by the project author through the TurboBench harness; no compiler or flags stated for that run (the standalone Makefile uses -O2). The independent powturbo Entropy Coder Benchmark figure is from a WebSearch snippet only, since sites.google.com is blocked here; its file, CPU and date were not seen. fsehuf compresses faster than fpc 32 (574.79 versus 548.16 MB/s), so the win is decode speed. Last commit April 2022. The older owner name algorithm314/FPC (still linked from TurboBench's README) redirects to kagiannis/FPC.

name: Huffman_coding_Gap_arrays (gap-array GPU Huffman)
baseline: Previously published GPU Huffman decoders (unnamed in the abstract summaries; the IPDPS 2022 artifact codyjrivera/ipdps22-opthuffdec benchmarks this decoder alongside CUHD's self-synchronization decoder), an unnamed CPU Huffman implementation, and the same GPU decoder without a gap array
workload: CUDA encoder and decoder implementing Huffman coding with gap arrays for GPU acceleration (ICPP 2020, DOI 10.1145/3404397.3404429).
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (WebSearch summaries of the ICPP 2020 abstract): GPU Huffman decoding 1.26x-2.63x faster (encoding 2.87x-7.70x faster) than previously presented GPU Huffman decoding (encoding); GPU decoding 35.2x-43.3x faster than CPU implementations; with a gap array attached, decoding is a further 1.67x-6450x faster than without one.
tradeoffs: Requires encoding with the gap array (extra stored data, not compatible with plain Huffman streams).
caveats: Repo README gives no numbers, compiler or hardware; no LICENSE, LICENSE.txt, LICENSE.md or COPYING at the root and none shown on the repo page (subdirectories not checked), so reference only. All numbers come from WebSearch summaries of the abstract; the paper, the github.io slides and the ACM PDF are blocked here. The CPU baseline is not named in the summaries. The 6450x upper bound compares against decoding without a gap array, i.e. the decoder's own fallback. Gap arrays change the encoded format, so it is not a drop-in decoder for plain Huffman streams. 9 commits, all between 2020-10-06 and 2020-10-09.

name: multians (massively parallel ANS decoding on GPUs)
baseline: 64-thread multicore CPU tANS decoder, a SIMD-based decoder and Zstandard's entropy codec
workload: GPU decoding of raw (unpartitioned) tANS-encoded streams using a self-synchronising overflow pattern; demo generates random 256-symbol data and compares GPU against multicore CPU decoding (ICPP 2019 paper, DOI 10.1145/3337821.3337888).
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (paper abstract via WebSearch): speedups of up to 17 over 64 CPU threads, up to 31 over a high-performance SIMD-based solution, and up to 39 over Zstandard's entropy codec.
tradeoffs: Requires CUDA GPU with compute capability 3.0+; the README demo is a synthetic uniform 256-symbol test, not the paper's datasets.

name: Recoil (parallel rANS decoding)
baseline: single-thread interleaved rANS, conventional fixed-partition parallel rANS, and the multians GPU ANS decoder (not zstd/lz4/zlib/brotli/xz)

tradeoffs: C++20 header-only library with CUDA support; GPL-3.0 copyleft; documentation 'TODO'. Test scripts and dataset in separate repo lin-toto/recoil-testscripts (submodules multians and recoil).

name: FiniteStateEntropy (FSE and Huff0)
baseline: zlibh (the Huffman encoder inside zlib, as packaged by Frederic Kayser)
workload: Compression and decompression of generated probability-distribution files (Proba80, Proba14, Proba02, made with the repo's probagen), 32 KB blocks.
claimed_speedup: Proba80: Huff0 1350 MB/s decode and 600 MB/s encode vs zlibh 300 / 265 MB/s (about 4.5x decode, 2.3x encode, derived); FSE 440 / 325 MB/s with ratio 8.84 vs 6.38 for Huffman and zlibh. Proba14: Huff0 860 vs zlibh 250 MB/s decode. Proba02: Huff0 555 vs zlibh 210 MB/s decode.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.8.4, 64-bit mode (optimisation flags not stated)
hardware: Intel Core i7-5600U, Linux Mint 64-bit
stars_or_usage: 1.5k stars; FSE and Huff0 are the entropy stage of zstd
tradeoffs: FSE is a table-based tANS coder (precise like arithmetic coding, but slower than Huff0); Huff0 is Huffman with 4-stream interleaving, loses ratio on skewed distributions (cannot go below 1 bit per symbol). Both are block-oriented with a header describing the distribution.
caveats: Benchmark is old (GCC 4.8.4, Broadwell laptop, optimisation flags not stated) and uses only synthetic generated distributions with 32 KB blocks. Baseline zlibh is a weak Huffman. Better modern Huffman decoders exist (see PIVCO-Huffman and hypersonic-rANS entries). zstd itself (facebook/zstd) is on the known list; this entry is the standalone upstream FSE/Huff0 repo, whose dev branch last changed 2024-03-10. The lib/ sources are dual BSD-2-Clause/GPLv2; the test and benchmark tools in programs/ are GPLv2 only.

name: Glyd
baseline: zstd -3 (also LZ4, zstd -19)
workload: Decompression of an 8.7 GB real-data corpus (logs, JSON events, SQL dumps, Parquet); the --max level uses 8-way interleaved Huffman literals and tANS sequences.
claimed_speedup: Suite 2026-09-21 (8.7 GB corpus of logs, JSON events, SQL dumps, Parquet), one thread, MB/s: Glyd --max ratio 3.98 decompresses 1,571 vs zstd -3 (ratio 3.86) 1,425 on Graviton3 (1.10x) but 1,287 vs 1,518 on Sapphire Rapids (0.85x, slower), and compresses at 233 vs 313 and 266 vs 377. Glyd default (ratio 2.82) decompresses 3,309 on Graviton3 and 2,752 on Sapphire Rapids vs LZ4 (ratio 2.72) 1,394 and 1,206, compressing at 332 vs 504 and 327 vs 456. Eight threads: Glyd default decompresses 22,707 MB/s and --max 10,413 vs zstd -3 1,422 and LZ4 1,392, but zstd and LZ4 frames are decoded on one thread. README summary: reads 3-7x faster than zstd on a server, writes at 0.71-0.77x zstd -3's speed.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.98, RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native', cargo release profile opt-level 3, lto fat, codegen-units 1; baselines libzstd 1.5.7 via the zstd crate (bulk API, in-process) and LZ4 via the lz4 crate's frame encoder/decoder; zstd 1.5.5 and lz4 1.9.4 CLIs from Ubuntu 24.04 for CLI rows.
hardware: AWS c7g.2xlarge (Graviton3, Neoverse V1, 8 vCPU) and c7i.2xlarge (Sapphire Rapids, Xeon Platinum 8488C, 8 vCPU), Ubuntu 24.04
license: BSD-3-Clause OR GPL-2.0 (codec); glyd-store and GPU package under BUSL-1.1
tradeoffs: Rust library with a C ABI, callable from C++. Higher ratio than LZ4 but lower than zstd at default level; compress speed 0.77x zstd -3 and 0.33x in record mode. Large parallel-decode gain needs the parallel-friendly Glyd framing, so output is not a drop-in zstd stream.
caveats: First party, very young repo (240 stars, 1 fork) with sweeping claims. Like-for-like (one thread, similar ratio) the decode win over zstd -3 is small and platform-dependent: 1.10x on Graviton3, 0.85x (slower) on Sapphire Rapids, and compression is slower than zstd -3 on both. The 22.7 GB/s headline compares 8-thread Glyd decoding with single-thread zstd/LZ4 frame decoding. The LZ4 baseline in examples/bench_suite.rs uses the lz4 crate's streaming frame Decoder with read_to_end, not the LZ4 block API, which likely explains LZ4 decoding at only about 1.4 GB/s; the README's 'each codec on its fastest API' does not hold for LZ4, so the LZ4 decode comparison is weak. Glyd writes a per-block checksum; zstd frames here carry none. Store and GPU parts are BUSL-1.1 (non-commercial free).

name: klauspost/compress fse and huff0 packages (Go tANS and Huffman)
baseline: Huffman (Go deflate Huffman coding stage)
workload: FSE (tANS) encoding and decoding of byte blocks of about 64 KB, per core, compared with deflate Huffman encoding and decoding on the same hardware.
claimed_speedup: README: deflate packages 'Typical speed is about 2x of the standard library packages' (no table; 'only minor speedup on decompression'); lzw '1.4-4x faster decompression and 1.1-2.7x faster compression' than compress/lzw. s2/README.md mixed web corpus (4,014,735,833 bytes, single goroutine): S2 936.73 MB/s at 73.60% reduction vs Snappy 790.15 MB/s at 71.89% and LZ4 452.02 MB/s at 73.50%; S2 Better 451.10 MB/s at 76.05%. Stream compression vs Snappy on a 16 core (32 thread) machine: 8.55x-22.00x using all threads (e.g. github-june-2days-2019.json 16.51x at 15224 MB/s, sofia csv 22.00x) because S2 streams compress concurrently and Snappy does not; on 1 CPU 0.88x-1.91x (slower than Snappy on 10gb.tar 0.97x and sharnd.out.2gb 0.88x; 'better' mode 0.27x-0.77x on 1 CPU).
hardware: unstated ("the same hardware")
tradeoffs: Go only, not callable from C++ without cgo. Block-level API with no integrity checks. Speed depends on block size and on the highest byte value in the input. The huff0 package (README at huff0/README.md) is a port of the Huff0 codec from FiniteStateEntropy; it carries no speed numbers of its own.
caveats: The baseline is Go's standard library, not C zlib; the ~2x deflate claim has no table and decompression gains are 'minor'. The 16-core S2 vs Snappy multiples mostly measure S2's concurrent stream compression against single-threaded Snappy; single-core S2 ranges 0.88x-1.91x and is slower than Snappy on two of ten files. No Go version or flags; CPU model not named for the compression table (Ryzen 3950X named only for decompression scaling); the LZ4 row in the corpus table does not name its implementation. LICENSE bundles BSD-3-Clause (main), Apache-2.0 and MIT sections for some subpackages/files (e.g. s2/cmd/internal/filepathx MIT), all OSI-approved.

name: MANS (Multi-byte ANS compressor)

workload: Compression and decompression of multi-byte (16/32-bit) integer scientific data; CPU run on an Intel Xeon Gold 5220S, GPU runs on NVIDIA A100 and AMD MI210; Adaptive Data Mapping converts multi-byte integers to 8-bit symbols before ANS.
claimed_speedup: CPU: 1.92x faster compression and 2.04x faster decompression vs FSE-ANS; 1.24x higher compression ratio than FSE-ANS in portable mode (README also lists 2.37x vs FSE-ANS in ratio mode). A100: 45.14x faster compression vs nvCOMP Huffman.

tradeoffs: Targets multi-byte integer data (HPC and sensor slices), not generic byte streams. Needs OpenMP; GPU paths need CUDA 12.6 or ROCm. The portable CPU mode trades some ratio for consistency with the GPU format.

name: ZipNN (Huffman-based lossless compression of AI model weights)
baseline: Zstandard (ZSTD v1.5.6, as written 'ZSTD v1.56' in the README table)
workload: Single-threaded compression and decompression of bfloat16 model weights in 256KB chunks: byte grouping then a C Huffman coder (the README says the bfloat16/float16 path is a C implementation with Huffman encoding), compared with plain ZSTD.
claimed_speedup: ZipNN v0.2.0 1120MB/s compression and 1660MB/s decompression at ratio 1.51 (66.3% output), versus ZSTD 785MB/s and 950MB/s at ratio 1.27 (78.3%); about 1.4x compress and 1.7x decompress speed (derived from page data). Multithreaded Xeon figure: up to 80GB/s decompression and 13GB/s compression with 16 workers.
compiler_and_flags: setup.py builds the C extension with -O3 -Wall -Wextra (compiler unstated); flags for the README table run are not stated
hardware: Table: unstated. 80GB/s multithreaded figure: Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ with 224 cores and two NUMA nodes.
tradeoffs: Only useful for floating-point model tensors (bfloat16, float16, float32, FP8); the speed and ratio win comes from byte grouping that separates the low-entropy exponent bytes, then Huffman, not from a faster general entropy coder. Python package with a C extension, so C++ use needs the C sources. Default configuration is ByteGrouping 4 with vanilla ZSTD.
caveats: First-party README table with no hardware, compiler, zstd level or benchmark script for the single-thread numbers; the table is for v0.2.0 (current 0.5.4) and labels zstd 'v1.56'. The C Huffman coder is not ZipNN's own: setup.py compiles Yann Collet's FiniteStateEntropy (huf_compress.c, huf_decompress.c, fse_*.c vendored under include/FiniteStateEntropy) and csrc/zipnn_core.c calls HUF_compress/HUF_decompress, i.e. the same Huffman family zstd uses for literals. The win over zstd comes from byte grouping (separating bfloat16 exponent bytes) plus Huffman-only coding, so the entropy-coder contribution is not isolated; category fit for entropy-coders is weak (domain-specific lossless compressor for model weights). Default configuration is byte grouping of 4 with vanilla zstd; method 'auto' picks zstd, lz4 or huffman. The LICENSE.txt is MIT but its copyright line names IBM and 'the Drain3 project contributors' (boilerplate copied from another IBM project). name: lzvolt
language: Rust (hand-written assembly decoders; C header and cdylib/staticlib callable from C++)
baseline: LZ4 (liblz4 decode and pack)
workload: Decode throughput on small values (records and varied data of 512 B, 4 KiB, 64 KiB, plus incompressible noise), codec vs liblz4 on its own format, same bytes and process, medians of three runs on three machines.
claimed_speedup: Decoding own format, GiB/s and margin over liblz4: varied 64 KiB 7.01 (+72%) Xeon 8481C, 8.40 (+64%) EPYC 9B14, 8.15 (+83%) Neoverse V2; records 512 B 9.44 (+29%), 10.78 (+33%), 10.60 (+22%); 18 of 18 cells +14% to +83%. Reading raw LZ4 blocks: ahead on 20 of 27 cells. Packing: ahead on 25 of 27 and smaller output.
tradeoffs: Own format is not LZ4-compatible (also reads LZ4 blocks). Encoder refuses data it cannot shrink by an eighth. Targets small values for caches and record stores, not large-file streaming. Per-CPU hand-written assembly; C API (include/lzvolt.h) is the only supported path from C++.
caveats: Brand-new single-author project with 0 stars (263 commits, extracted from the author's KevaVolt project); latest commit 2026-10-02 corrected a misattributed capacity x throughput table in the README (the M2 column had been dropped and labels shifted), which does not affect the decode/pack tables quoted here. Throughput is counted against unpacked bytes, so smaller output inflates the number. Packing is not ahead on varied_4k Neoverse V2 (-2%) or varied_64k EPYC (+0%). Reading raw LZ4 blocks loses on 7 of 27 cells, worst noise_512 on x86 (-15% Xeon, -12% EPYC); the author attributes this to buffer-placement sensitivity. Rust with hand-written assembly; usable from C++ only through its C ABI (include/lzvolt.h, staticlib/cdylib); assembly kernels only on Linux/macOS x86-64 and aarch64, portable Rust elsewhere. name: ZXC
baseline: LZ4 (fast, default, HC -9) and zstd -1
workload: Single-threaded decompression speed on the Silesia corpus (202 MB) at matched ratio tiers, measured with lzbench 2.3.1 on four machines.
claimed_speedup: Decompression speed ratio ZXC vs competitor at each tier (Apple M2 / Axion Neoverse-V2 / EPYC 9B45 / EPYC 7B13): -1 vs lz4 --fast 2.62x / 1.92x / 2.20x / 1.81x; -3 vs lz4 1.75x / 1.41x / 1.36x / 1.22x; -6 vs lz4hc -9 1.50x / 1.25x / 1.19x / 1.10x; -7 vs zstd -1 2.60x / 1.94x / 2.21x / 2.13x. Ratio also slightly smaller output in each pairing (e.g. 61.76% vs 62.15%).
stars_or_usage: 465 stars, 11 forks; zxc 0.14.1 is integrated in lzbench (listed 2026-09-20) and TurboBench (listed as added 2026/05)
tradeoffs: Asymmetric: slow encoder (optimal parsing) for fast decoder, aimed at write-once/read-many data. Compression speed is lower than LZ4 at the fast tier. Bindings for Rust, Python, Node.js, Go, WASM. Optional seekable archives.
caveats: README numbers are first party, but code, tool (lzbench), flags and CPUs are public and the CI benchmark workflow re-runs lzbench on ubuntu-latest and macos-26-xlarge. Independent check: the lzbench README (lzbench 2.4, gcc 15.2.0, single thread of AMD EPYC 9555P, turbo off) lists zxc 0.14.1 -1 at 8151 MB/s decode vs lz4 --fast -17 3977 MB/s (2.05x), -3 4716 vs lz4 3832 MB/s (1.23x), -6 3938 vs lz4hc -9 3703 MB/s (1.06x), with ratios 61.76/46.09/36.28% vs 62.15/47.60/36.75% (ratios derived from page data); zxc -7 is not in that table. The x86 gain at the high tier is small (1.06-1.19x); the win is largest on ARM64. Compression is much slower than LZ4 at -6 (9.04 vs 31.9 MB/s for lz4hc -9 in lzbench). Another repo (Vladexy88x/zxc) shows the same description and appears to be a copy. Repo is young.

name: BriefLZ
baseline: zlib (zlib 1.2.11 in the README table, zlib 1.3.2 in lzbench 2.4)
workload: Silesia corpus through lzbench, compression and decompression speed and ratio at several levels, compared with brotli, zstd, zlib, lz4hc and lzo.
claimed_speedup: README table (Core i5-4570 at 3.2 GHz): brieflz 1.3.0 -6 compresses at 17 MB/s and decompresses at 400 MB/s with ratio 31.71; zlib 1.2.11 -9 does 11 MB/s and 320 MB/s with ratio 31.92 (about 1.5x faster compression and 1.25x faster decompression, derived from page data). lzbench 2.4 (EPYC 9555P): brieflz -6 22.8 MB/s and 328 MB/s versus zlib -9 11.3 MB/s and 318 MB/s (2.0x compression, 1.03x decompression, derived).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.0 (lzbench 2.4 release binary lzbench24_x86_64-linux-gnu-gcc15); lzbench v2.4 Makefile OPT_FLAGS_O3: -fomit-frame-pointer -fstrict-aliasing -O3 -DNDEBUG (a few codecs use the -O2 variant); run options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4

tradeoffs: Very small code (compressor 147 lines, decompressor 61 lines); no entropy coding; has no window size limit, so it needs the whole buffer.
caveats: Decompression gain over zlib is marginal (3% in lzbench 2.4, 25% in the 2020 README table). At matched levels the picture is mixed: brieflz -6 (22.8 MB/s, 31.71%) compresses slower than zlib -6 (26.8 MB/s, 32.19%) for a 1.5% smaller output; the clear wins are brieflz -6 vs zlib -9 and brieflz -3 (124 / 301 MB/s, 35.65%) vs zlib -1 (89.0 / 297 MB/s, 36.45%), derived from page data. The README says its comparison 'is not entirely fair because BriefLZ has no window size limit'. zstd and brotli beat it at similar ratios, and zlib-ng/libdeflate are not compared. Tier B rests on the third-party lzbench 2.4 table; the README table is first-party and lacks compiler flags.

hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04

workload: Compression of short strings (22 'dbtext' data sets, each an 8 MB file, single-threaded) with random access per string; LZ4 used in file-based mode.
claimed_speedup: PVLDB 2020 paper Table 1 (22 dbtext sets, 8 MB files, single thread): FSST compression speed beats LZ4 on 21 of 22 sets (e.g. genome 1,307 vs 566 MB/s, uuid 1,113 vs 632, credentials 984 vs 439; LZ4 wins on hex 1,097 vs 944) with a higher compression factor on 21 of 22 (e.g. genome 3.32 vs 1.59, uuid 2.44 vs 1.55; LZ4 wins on urls 2.77 vs 2.16); paper text gives average factor 2.28x vs LZ4 1.70x. Decompression speed is mixed: FSST faster on 12 sets (e.g. genome 2,838 vs 1,126 MB/s, c_name 3,519 vs 2,960), LZ4 faster on 10 (e.g. hex 1,891 vs 1,546, email 2,388 vs 1,547) (counts derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Strings only (symbol table of up to 8-byte symbols mapped to 1-byte codes); static table per block, random access to single strings without block decode; not a general-purpose byte-stream compressor. Best on short-string columns, ratio gain largest on machine-generated IDs.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (PVLDB vol 13 no 12, 2020); numbers read from the paper PDF checked into the repo (via raw.githubusercontent.com). LZ4 version is old (1.8.1) with g++ 8.3.1. Decompression is on par with LZ4, slower on 10 of 22 sets; the main win is compression ratio, compression speed and per-string random access. File mode is LZ4's best case per the paper. Replication package (paper/ directory with dbtext corpus and Makefile) is in the repo; it needs Linux perf counters and LZ4 1.8.1 on PATH.

name: Rapidgzip
baseline: GNU gzip (single-threaded deflate decoder); also compared with pigz, igzip (ISA-L), bgzip and pzstd
workload: Decompression of arbitrary gzip files (Silesia tar repeated 20x, 3.95 GiB; 4 GiB base64 data) on a Ryzen 3900X, plus scaling to 128 cores on 2x EPYC 7702.
claimed_speedup: Ryzen 3900X, 20x-silesia with existing index: 5640 MB/s (0 threads=auto) vs gzip 293 MB/s (18.8x); from scratch 2070 MB/s (6.9x); 4GiB-base64 from scratch 5060 MB/s vs gzip 250 MB/s (20.1x). README: up to 24 GB/s with index and 12 GB/s without on 128 cores; 24.3 GB/s vs 9.5 GB/s for pzstd with index. Paper abstract: 5.6 GB/s on Silesia, speedup 33 over GNU gzip, with 128 cores. README: single-core decompression close to igzip and about twice as fast as bgzip (zlib).
license: Apache-2.0 AND MIT (repo page lists both; per-file split not checked)
tradeoffs: Multi-core only wins: single-thread speed is close to igzip, not faster. Needs memory for chunk cache and a two-stage decode of unknown windows; with an index it reaches higher bandwidth. Read-only decompressor (compression is delegated to other tools). C++17, usable as header-only C++ library.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (ACM HPDC 2023, DOI 10.1145/3588195.3592992); the paper PDF in mxmlnkn/indexed_bzip2/results/paper was opened, but neither it nor the README states the compiler or flags. The headline gain is parallel scaling versus single-threaded GNU gzip, not a faster single-thread inflate: in the paper (rapidgzip 0.5.0), single-threaded rapidgzip reached 153 MB/s, while bgzip was 1.9x and igzip 4.3x as fast; the README's claim that single-core speed is close to igzip refers to later versions. Baseline is GNU gzip rather than zlib. The README scaling plots used rapidgzip 0.9.0, and its values are higher than the paper's. The paper's text gives GNU gzip on Silesia as "172 GB/s", an evident typo for MB/s.

name: blz4
baseline: lz4 (lz4 -12 -l, legacy format)

caveats: Not a speed win: the README itself says lz4 'does flexible parsing, is very close to optimal, and much faster', and calls the project 'a quick experiment ... not production quality, and has not been properly tested'. name: c-blosc2 (Blosc2 shuffle+lz4)
baseline: memcpy (uncompressed copy); inner codecs lz4/zstd/zlib are components, not rivals
workload: Repo bench suite (bench/b2bench.c) on 4 MiB synthetic 32-bit data with 19 significant bits, shuffle filter plus LZ4 codec, 256 MB working set, 8 threads: compressed-chunk read and write versus plain memcpy of the same buffer.
claimed_speedup: At 8 threads, lz4+shuffle clevel 1 (ratio 4.75): decompression 31337.5 MB/s vs memcpy(read) 8962.2 MB/s, and compression 13172.7 MB/s vs memcpy(write) 9641.2 MB/s (derived from page data: about 3.5x on decode and 1.4x on encode). At 16 threads, clevel 1: decomp 28495.0 MB/s and comp 19772.6 MB/s vs memcpy read 9311.2 / write 9828.8 MB/s (the 35428.1 MB/s figure is clevel 0, ratio 1.00, i.e. no compression). Single thread clevel 1 decode (5293.7 MB/s) is slower than memcpy(read) (8581.6 MB/s), and compression (2066.7 MB/s) is slower than memcpy(write) (4691.4 MB/s).
hardware: Host named only 'corex' in the output (CPU model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 586 stars; used by PyTables, h5py, Zarr per README
tradeoffs: Meta-compressor: needs typed, regular binary data (shuffle/bitshuffle filters) to win; gains come from multithreading and cache effects; chunked frame format and NDim layer add API surface.
caveats: Result file is from Blosc 2.0.0.beta.6 (2020) with LZ4 1.9.3 and Zstd 1.4.9; CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated (first-party, tier C). The baseline is memcpy only: bench/ (b2bench.c, sum_openmp.c, sframe_bench.c, delta_schunk.c, zero_runlen.c and others) has no benchmark against standalone lz4/zstd/zlib, and the one README plot (images/Read-Partial-Slices-B2ND.png) compares the Python NDArray slicing (2.25/1.34/0.75/0.5 GB/s) against Zarr with Blosc1 and HDF5 via h5py-Blosc2, not against a codec. Data is synthetic. An independent blog (Aras Pranckevicius, 'Float Compression 8: Blosc', 2023) says, per a WebSearch snippet only (the site is blocked here), that Blosc defaults beat plain zstd (slightly higher ratio, faster compression, much faster decompression) and mostly beat plain lz4 (much better ratio, faster compression, slightly slower decompression); no numbers were read and its Blosc version is unconfirmed. The zstd sum_openmp output in the same folder shows compressed-in-memory summation slower than uncompressed (1582 MB/s vs 11818 MB/s at 1 thread). The Blosc2 blog, Blosc2-Debunking-Myths.pdf (blosc.org) and the SciPy NDim paper were blocked.

name: Chromium zlib (third_party/zlib fork)
baseline: zlib (upstream madler/zlib)
workload: Inflate of gzip and zlib-wrapped streams (snappy corpus), raw CRC-32, and PNG decoding with SSE4.2/PCLMUL crc32, adler32 SIMD and chunk-copy inflate.
claimed_speedup: CRC-32 5x-25x faster than zlib's default BYFOUR crc32; gzip- and zlib-wrapped inflate 69% and 50% faster on the snappy corpus; PNG 140 corpus decoding rate 4% faster on average from crc32 alone, 40% total combined with adler32 SIMD and inflate chunk copy. Later commits report gains over the previous Chromium zlib, not upstream: the ANZAC++ hash gives 30-40% faster compression (M1 31.3%, SPR 41.9%; 0.1% ratio loss on snappy) and overlapped bitstream refill gives an 8.09% average inflate gain across 7 CPUs (EPYC 9B45 7.86%, EPYC 9B14 11.21%, Xeon 8481C 6.16%, Axion 8.89%, Ryzen 9 9900X 8.77%, Cortex-X3 5.53%, Cortex-X4 10.13%).
compiler_and_flags: SSE4.2 and PCLMUL for the SIMD crc32 code (selected at run time); since Aug 2026 the SIMD ISA is set per function via __target__. Benchmark compiler and flags not stated in the commits.
stars_or_usage: Ships in Chrome; github.com/chromium/chromium mirror 24.9k stars
tradeoffs: Tied to Chromium's build (BUILD.gn, runtime CPU detection, symbol renaming via names.h); x86, Arm and RISC-V SIMD paths; heavily patched inflate (inffast_chunk) means it does not track upstream zlib cleanly.
caveats: Headline numbers come from a first-party commit message (the 2018 SSE4.2 crc32 change) with no CPU model, compiler or flags; its details are on crbug.com/796178, which was blocked here. Newer commits (ANZAC++ hash 2023, bitstream-refill overlap 2026-09-22) name CPUs but measure against the previous Chromium zlib, not upstream madler/zlib, and do not state the tool or flags. A public harness exists at third_party/zlib/contrib/bench/zlib_bench.cc. This is a distinct fork from Cloudflare zlib (an independent fork) and zlib-ng (a separate project that adopted some Chromium ideas such as chunk copy), with its own code (*simd* files, contrib/optimizations) and its own evidence, so it is not a duplicate. The repo URL is the whole Chromium mirror; the code is in third_party/zlib (canonical: chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/third_party/zlib). Synced to zlib 1.3.2.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Chromium zlib optimizations SIMD inflate crc32 faster than zlib blog'; commit opened via the github.com mirror (chromium.googlesource.com is egress-blocked).

name: em_inflate
baseline: zlib (inflate 1.2.11)
workload: Memory-to-memory decompression of enwik8 (gzip -9 bitstream, 100,000,000 bytes to 36,445,248) and a 32,212,992-byte raw texture file (zlib bitstream, gzip -9 to 13,721,537).
claimed_speedup: enwik8: zlib inflate 1.2.11 426,167 us, em_inflate with checksum 358,118 us (84%), skipping checksum 275,847 us (64%); texture: 127,945 us vs 114,369 us (89%) vs 105,476 us (82%). Derived from page data: about 1.19x and 1.54x on enwik8, 1.12x and 1.21x on the texture file.
tradeoffs: Single file em_inflate.c/.h, single function call, memory-to-memory only: no streaming API, so it is not a drop-in replacement for the zlib inflate stream interface. Needs the whole input and output buffers in memory. Under 1,200 lines including about 300 lines of checksum code. The headline 64% needs checksum verification skipped, which gives up integrity checking.
caveats: First-party README numbers only. CPU model, compiler flags for the timing run, repeat counts and the benchmark harness are not given. Baseline is zlib 1.2.11 (2017), not a current zlib or zlib-ng/libdeflate, which are much faster than stock zlib at inflate. The README with these numbers was last updated in June 2019 ('Faster codeword reversal. Update README.'); robustness fixes followed (buffer overflow fix August 2020, merged October 2020), so the timings predate those fixes; the only 2022 commits are cosmetic (error-message style, commenting out unused code). The 'skip checksum' row does not verify integrity, so the like-for-like gain versus zlib (which verifies) is the 84%/89% row. License: zlib license, with the gzip crc32 code by Stephan Brumme under a zlib-like license, per README. Original that inflatecpp ports.

name: fast_zlib
baseline: zlib 1.2.11 (stock deflate, level 9)
workload: Compression at level 9 of Unreal Engine 4 source code (137 MB), UE4 Win64 binaries, and graphics files (TIF/PNG geometry and textures) up to 256 MB; also the Silesia corpus (202.1 MB).
claimed_speedup: Wiki Release 2 (VS 2019), level 9, C version vs original zlib: source code 5.1 s vs 10.7 s (28,858,611 vs 28,859,103 bytes); binaries 12.6 s vs 49.1 s (54,473,779 vs 54,485,836 bytes); geometry 18.2 s vs 180.0 s (114,915,875 vs 114,942,962 bytes). Wiki states the optimized version 'performs nearly 2.5-10 times faster'. Silesia (202.1 MB) level 9: 20.90 vs 8.51 MB/s; level 5: 29.82 vs 29.23 MB/s; level 1: 63.52 vs 62.10 MB/s. Derived from page data: 2.1x, 3.9x and 9.9x on the three level-9 sets, about 2.5x on Silesia level 9, about 1.02x at levels 5 and 1.
tradeoffs: Replaces only longest_match in deflate.c (C version or 32-bit x86 NASM assembly); zlib 1.2.13+ needs a patch because ASMV was removed upstream. Output format stays standard deflate, so any inflater reads it. Wiki says compressed sizes are equal to original zlib; the README says 'slightly smaller'.
caveats: First-party numbers on an old laptop CPU (i7-4702MQ, Windows 8.1) with MSVC; the key datasets (UE4 source, binaries, geometry/textures) are the author's own and are not published, and optimization flags are not given. The gain is only at high levels: on Silesia at levels 5 and 1 it is about 2% (29.82 vs 29.23 MB/s, 63.52 vs 62.10 MB/s). Baseline is zlib 1.2.11 only; no comparison with zlib-ng, libdeflate or Cloudflare/Intel zlib forks. It replaces zlib's longest_match only; zlib 1.2.13+ removed ASMV, so it needs the bundled patch (Sources/zlib_1.2.13.patch). Compressed output is slightly smaller than stock zlib output, not byte-identical to it.

name: fflate
baseline: pako (JavaScript port of zlib); README also says its compressor beats Info-ZIP and often zlib's ratio
workload: DEFLATE, gzip, zlib and ZIP compression and decompression in JavaScript (Node and browsers)
claimed_speedup: README table (pako = 1x): decompression 'Up to 25% faster', compression 'Up to 50% faster'; text says about 25% faster than UZIP.js. Sync ZIP compression 'compresses both more quickly and with a higher compression ratio than most compression software (even Info-ZIP, a C program)'; async mode 'over 3x the performance of virtually any other utility'. Against native zlib (Node bindings) the README itself says fflate is 'around 30% slower in decompression and 10% slower in compression'.
tradeoffs: Pure JavaScript, so usable from C++ only through an embedded JS engine; 8 kB bundle; async mode uses Web Workers with about 50 ms start overhead per function; the README says outputs are checked to be no more than 5% larger than competitors at max compression.
caveats: The win is against pako (a JS port of zlib), not native zlib: the README states fflate is about 30% slower than native zlib in decompression and 10% slower in compression, and that the native CompressionStream API ranges from 30% faster to 10% slower. Only 'up to' percentages, no data, Node version, CPU or flags; results of npm test (test/results) are not published. The 'beats Info-ZIP' and '3x' statements are unsupported by tables. Worth listing as the fast pure-JS option where native zlib is unavailable (browsers without a sync API).
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/zlib page

verification.notes: Kept as a JS-ecosystem entry: faster than pako, but by its own README slower than native zlib, which matters for a catalog benchmarked against zlib. Metadata checked: MIT (SheetJS-derived part 0BSD), about 3.0k stars, not archived, not a fork; last commit 2026-05-16 (v0.8.3).

name: Firetrail (formerly skim)
baseline: lz4 (also zstd)
workload: End-to-end CLI runs (file in, file out, warm page cache), single thread, on silesia.tar, HDFS.log, enwik8 and enwik9.
claimed_speedup: Silesia: Firetrail White encodes at 1.67 GB/s and Orange at 1.54 GB/s versus lz4 1.10.0 --fast=20 at 0.98 GB/s and zstd 1.5.7 --fast=5 at 0.69 GB/s; geometric mean over four corpora: White 1.6x faster than lz4 and 2.5x faster than zstd on encode. Orange ratio on silesia 1.54x versus lz4 1.56x. Independent lzbench row for the earlier skim 0.1.0: 2313 MB/s compress, 3500 MB/s decompress, ratio 64.53% versus lz4 --fast -17 at 924 and 3977 MB/s and 62.15%.
compiler_and_flags: Firetrail built with Zig in release-fast mode (README: zig build bench --release=fast); the end-to-end tables come from scripts/bench.fish, which times the firetrail, zstd and lz4 CLIs with poop. Baseline zstd 1.5.7 and lz4 1.10.0 are system binaries with no build flags stated.
hardware: Ryzen 7 7800X3D, CachyOS, single thread
tradeoffs: Density-inspired 8-byte word hash with a 512 KB table; ratio is low (1.3-1.5x on silesia). White needs a trained dictionary. Streaming with 15-20 MB RSS. Written in Zig; no C API is mentioned.
caveats: Baselines are non-default fast settings (lz4 --fast=20, zstd --fast=5), both -T1. White's figures use a 512 KB dictionary trained by Red on the very input being compressed and not counted in the output size, which flatters White's ratio and is not a deployable setup; Orange (cold, no dictionary) is the fair comparison. lz4 still decodes faster on every corpus (2.53 GB/s versus 1.89 GB/s White on silesia), and lz4 and zstd compress smaller on silesia and HDFS.log. enwik8 nearly fits the 96 MB L3, which the author says flatters it. No LICENSE file in the repo, so code must not be copied. The old skim repo only shows a migration notice pointing to Firetrail; the lzbench row is for skim 0.1.0, an earlier codec version.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): lzbench README 2.4 table (skim 0.1.0 row, which led to the skim repo and its Firetrail successor)

name: Gipfeli
baseline: zlib
workload: Single core of a Core i7 in 64-bit mode; workload not specified in the README.
claimed_speedup: Compresses at about 180 MB/s or more and decompresses at about 300 MB/s, typically 5x faster than zlib, with about 30% fewer bytes than other high-speed libraries for text.
hardware: Core i7 (model not stated), single core
tradeoffs: Snappy-class speed with an entropy stage; does not reach zlib's density. Written in C++ with no assembly.
caveats: First-party README claim with no workload, compiler, flags or exact CPU; the README does not say whether the 5x refers to compression or decompression speed, and it concedes Gipfeli does not reach zlib's compression density. name: Inflate++ (inflatecpp)
baseline: zlib inflate 1.2.11
workload: Decompress a zlib stream of a large raw texture (60,132,846 bytes compressed to 25,614,357) and a gzip archive (147,120,395 bytes compressed to 53,625,384), memory to memory; time in microseconds.
claimed_speedup: zlib bitstream: zlib inflate 1.2.11 134,245 us (100%); Inflate++ with checksum 118,399 us (91%); without checksum 110,238 us (85%). gzip bitstream: zlib 465,567 us (100%); Inflate++ with checksum 362,133 us (87%); without checksum 265,462 us (65%). About 1.13x (zlib) and 1.29x (gzip) faster with checksum, 1.22x and 1.75x without (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Single-call, memory-to-memory decompressor under 1000 lines of C++ plus about 250 lines of Adler-32; no streaming API mentioned.
caveats: No CPU, compiler, flags or benchmark harness; two inputs only. The README's percentage column does not match its own times (e.g. 362,133/465,567 is 78%, not 87%; 265,462/465,567 is 57%, not 65%), so the table was edited carelessly. The 'without checksum' rows skip verification that zlib performs, so they are not like-for-like. Baseline zlib 1.2.11 is old; zlib-ng and libdeflate are far faster than both. Windows-only build script; no tests in repo.

name: Intel QPL (IAA hardware deflate path)
baseline: zlib-ng and zstd software compression (Intel RocksDB guide); Snappy and CPU deflate execution in DuckDB (ADMS 2025 paper)
workload: RocksDB compression/decompression with Intel IAA offload on 4th-gen Xeon (per Intel tuning guide), plus DuckDB and HTSlib tests in third-party papers.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only, no page opened. ADMS 2025 paper ('A Hot Take on the Intel Analytics Accelerator for Database Management Systems') per search snippet: DuckDB Deflate on IAA reaches 4.59 GB/s compression and 18.24 GB/s decompression; up to 10x faster decompression than DuckDB's Snappy in microbenchmarks and up to 30% lower end-to-end TPC-H query latency. Intel RocksDB tuning guide per search snippet: 103% higher throughput and 64% lower p99 latency than zstd for an 80:20 read/write mix with 16KB blocks and 256B values (this differs from the 34%-95% / 23%-51% range in the original record; neither could be checked against the page). The zlib-ng figures (92%-205% throughput, 53%-74% p99) were not confirmed by any snippet this verifier saw.
hardware: Intel Sapphire Rapids Xeon (4th gen) with IAA accelerator
tradeoffs: Needs IAA hardware on Sapphire Rapids or later for the fast path; software fallback is the only option elsewhere. Deflate format only, ratio is lower than zstd. Related shim intel/zlib-accel (Apache-2.0) offloads whole-stream zlib calls to QAT/IAA or igzip but ships no benchmarks and has no streaming support on the accelerators.
caveats: Hardware-gated: the speedups come from the Intel IAA accelerator on 4th-gen Xeon (Sapphire Rapids) and later, a different machine class from a software codec; QPL's software fallback path has no published comparison against zlib-ng or zstd. name: jtkukunas/zlib (Intel zlib fork)
baseline: zlib (stock deflate)
workload: Compression speed at levels 1, 5/6 and 7-9 on HTML, executables, JPEG and PNG pixel data, as reported by a third-party blog comparing the Intel and Cloudflare zlib forks with stock zlib.
claimed_speedup: Third-party blog (Snellman 2014, read through WebSearch snippets only): at level 1, Intel's 'quick' strategy takes 36% of baseline time on an executable (Cloudflare fork 70%), but its compressed size grows to 0.46 of the original against 0.37 for baseline. At level 5 ('medium' strategy) it takes 0.99 s against a 1.76 s baseline on the executable (56% of baseline time), and 0.75 s against 0.69 s on JPEG (108%, slower on uncompressible data). Derived from page data: about 2.8x faster at level 1 and 1.8x at level 5 on the executable. The claims that levels 7-9 are slightly behind Cloudflare and that decompression is slower than Cloudflare's were not re-confirmed in this run.
tradeoffs: Fork of zlib adding SSE4.2 crc32 hashing, PCLMULQDQ CRC folding, deflate_quick (level 1) and deflate_medium (levels 4-5). Compression ratio is lower at level 1 (new speed/ratio point) and about equal at level 5. x86 only; archived by Intel with a notice that it is no longer maintained. Repo HEAD is rebased on zlib 1.2.13 per its README and zlib.h.
caveats: The benchmark blog (snellman.net) is egress-blocked, so its figures were checked only through WebSearch snippets: level 1 at 36% of baseline time with a worse ratio (0.46 vs 0.37), and level 5 at 0.99 s vs 1.76 s on an executable and 0.75 s vs 0.69 s on JPEG. The harness is public at github.com/jsnell/zlib-bench, but its README names no compiler, flags or CPU; the i7-4770 comes from a snippet. The blog measured the 2014 state of the fork, not the later 1.2.13 rebase. The repo was archived on 2024-03-01 with Intel's 'no longer maintained' notice. Superseded by zlib-ng (already catalogued): zlib-ng's README says it has 'Deflate medium and quick algorithms based on Intel's zlib fork' and 'Includes improvements from Cloudflare and Intel forks', and its author says he 'merge[d] all the Intel optimizations'. Use zlib-ng instead; keep this entry for history and attribution. The level-1 'quick' strategy trades compression ratio for speed. The license is the standard zlib license (LICENSE file read).

name: liblzraven
baseline: xz
workload: Decoding 89.7 MiB of OS 27 over-the-air payloads, measured with tools/benchmark.py; also a synthetic corpus on Apple M4 Pro.
claimed_speedup: x86-64 (Ryzen 9 7950X, AVX2 path): decoder 1.96x xz -6 throughput per the README (SPEC.md section 12.4: 2182 versus 1096 MiB/s size-weighted, 1.99x; dense subset 1071 versus 642 MiB/s, 1.67x) on 89.7 MiB of real OS 27 OTA payloads, at ratio on par with xz -6 (10 wins, 9 losses, 1 tie; Apple's encoder produced the streams); decoder memory 35,336 bytes versus 8.06 MiB for liblzma at -6. Apple M4 Pro NEON path: 954 MiB/s versus xz -6 at 328 MiB/s (2.91x) on a substitute corpus.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2 at -O2 with run-time SIMD dispatch (avx2 selected) on x86-64; Apple clang 21 at -O2 on the M4 Pro; liblzma 5.8.1 and zlib 1.3.1 (x86) and liblzma 5.8.3 (M4 Pro) as baselines, their build flags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (Zen 4), Linux 6.12, single pinned core for the x86 tables; Apple M4 Pro (10P + 4E), macOS 27.0 for the NEON table
tradeoffs: Clean-room C11 decoder and encoder of Apple's LZRAVEN codec (LZ + rANS) for OTA payloads; buffer-only, no streaming, no allocation in the decoder. Encoder is slow (about 70 MB/s on redundant data, 4-20 MB/s otherwise).
caveats: Measured on a niche corpus of OS payloads that compress 29.9x; the ratio parity with xz -6 is for streams written by Apple's encoder, while this library's own encoder is about 4% larger than Apple's. On the dense subset zlib -6 decodes faster (1282 MiB/s) than liblzraven (1071 MiB/s), though at much lower ratio (8.85x versus 13.77x). The x86 corpus is carved from Apple OTA payloads and is not redistributable, so only the M4 Pro table (built with tools/make_corpus.py, which needs Apple's native encoder) can be reproduced from public data. The README admits Apple's own decoder is faster (1333 versus 954 MiB/s). The repo is entirely AI-authored and the owner says he does not intend to maintain it; one commit (2026-07-30). Compared against xz and zlib only, not zstd. The format has no integrity checks. TurboBench lists it as an Apple lzraven reimplementation.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): TurboBench codec list (lzraven added 2026/09)

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded from C: SPEC.md section 12 gives the full method for the README's numbers: public harness tools/benchmark.py, decoder built with GCC 14.2 at -O2 (AVX2 selected at run time), AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, Linux 6.12, against liblzma 5.8.1 and zlib 1.3.1 on the same machine, best of 9 pinned to one core; the M4 Pro table uses tools/bench_apple.py, Apple clang 21 at -O2, against liblzma 5.8.3 on a corpus built by tools/make_corpus.py. Code, compiler, flags and CPU model are all stated, so A, with the caveat that the x86 corpus (Apple OTA payloads) is not redistributable.

baseline: xz and 7z (LZMA), plus bzip2 and gzip
workload: Compress a Linux 2.6.37 kernel tarball (430,612,480 bytes) with default options; also six consecutive kernel trees (2.37 GB).
tradeoffs: Needs large RAM for long-range dedup window; wins mainly on large files with distant redundancy (hundreds of MB apart). Multithreaded across blocks, so wall-clock gains come partly from using 4 cores against single-threaded xz.

Wall-time comparison with lrzip using all cores against xz of that era (single-threaded) and 7z. Modern multithreaded xz (-T) and zstd --long would narrow or reverse the gap. Author's own benchmark. lrzip is a file-level CLI (rzip long-range pass plus LZMA/LZO/ZPAQ backends), 64-bit only, and wins mostly on large inputs with long-distance redundancy.

name: lz4ultra
baseline: lz4 (lz4 1.9.2 -12 high-compression encoder, same LZ4 format)
workload: Decompression time for enwik9 (1,000,000,000 bytes) of LZ4-format streams produced by lz4 -12 versus lz4ultra's optimal packer.
claimed_speedup: README table (enwik9, Core i7-6700): lz4ultra 1.3.0 --favor-decSpeed output (376,118,079 bytes) decompresses in 296,972 microseconds versus 457,141 microseconds for lz4 1.9.2 -12 --favor-decSpeed output (377,175,400 bytes), 1.54x faster (derived from page data); favor-ratio output 347,936 versus 505,804 microseconds (1.45x, derived) with 371,680,323 versus 372,443,347 compressed bytes (lz4ultra versus lz4).
hardware: Core i7-6700 (as printed in the README table)
tradeoffs: Output is plain LZ4 format, readable by the standard lz4 decoder; the gain comes from fewer tokens, not from a faster decoder. Compression is an offline optimal parse and slower than lz4 -12 (no timing given).
caveats: First-party numbers, one dataset, no compiler flags, and the README does not say which decoder produced the timings (it says files are meant to be decompressed with lz4 and that its own decompressor is not as optimized as lz4 proper). Compared against lz4 1.9.2 (2019), not the current 1.10.0. smalLZ4 1.5 -9 in the same table is essentially identical in favor-ratio mode (371,680,328 bytes, 348,018 microseconds). Last commit 2023-01-29, more than 3 years ago. CC0 matchfinder carries no patent grant; it bundles libdivsufsort (MIT).

name: LZSA
baseline: LZ4_HC (lz4)
workload: Compression ratio and relative decompression speed on a ZX Spectrum/C64 file set (1,289,127 bytes) plus Canterbury, Silesia, Calgary, Large and enwik9 corpora; speed measured on 8-bit Z80/6502 decompressors.
claimed_speedup: README table 'Decompression speed vs. LZ4' (ZX Spectrum/C64 file set): LZSA1 90%, LZSA2 75%, LZ4_HC -19 -B4 -BD 100%, i.e. slower than LZ4 at default settings. The README's pareto_graph.png (ZX Spectrum, decompression rate in bytes per frame) plots the fastest LZSA1 variants (LZSA1-m4, LZSA1-m5) at about 2,400-2,570 bytes/frame against about 2,170-2,360 for the two LZ4 decompressors, roughly 9% faster at the top end (derived from page data, read off the graph, approximate), while also compressing better. Compression ratio beats LZ4_HC -19 on every listed corpus, e.g. Silesia LZSA1 34.78% and LZSA2 32.52% versus LZ4_HC 36.47%; enwik9 35.54% / 33.49% versus 37.18%. hardware: 8-bit micros (Z80, 6502, 8088); host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Targets 8-bit decompressors in assembly; the host-side packer is portable C (matchfinder.c is CC0 from wimlib) but compression is about 2x slower than LZ4_HC. Not a modern x86/Arm speed play.
caveats: The speed win exists only for 8-bit decompressors (Z80 graph) and only for the speed-tuned LZSA1 modes; the README's own table reads slower than LZ4 on decompression (90% and 75%), and the compressor is about 2x slower than LZ4_HC, so on modern CPUs this is a ratio win, not a speed win. No host CPU, compiler, flags or benchmark harness; the graph values are approximate readings. Licensing is mixed but all OSI/CC0: Zlib for the code, CC0 for src/matchfinder.c (no patent grant for that file). Last commit 2023-02-27, over 3 years old.

name: OpenZL

claimed_speedup: Release notes v0.3.0 (opened): on Silesia, OpenZL LZ v0.3.0 ratio 2.73, compression 467 MB/s, decompression 3062 MB/s vs zstd ratio 2.74, 419 MB/s, 1254 MB/s ("144% faster" decoding than zstd "at equivalent settings"); a Compression Transformer table on 868 numeric stream families (17.9 GB) reports ratio 7.76x vs zstd -19 5.752x and xz -9 5.920x (ratio, not speed). tradeoffs: Wins come from describing the data format and training a compressor graph; decompression of format-aware streams is slower than zstd; API and format subject to change off release tags; requires C11 and C++17.

name: orz

name: pugz
baseline: GNU gunzip (gzip); libdeflate also compared in the paper
workload: Parallel decompression of gzip-compressed ASCII text files (FASTQ in the paper; 2.7 GB and 24 GB compressed files in the README), speed measured in compressed input bytes per second

Paper Table II (32 threads, FASTQ files preloaded in memory): gunzip 37 MB/s, libdeflate 118 MB/s, pugz 611 MB/s, stated as 16.5x faster than gunzip and 5.2x faster than libdeflate
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: -std=c++11 -mssse3 -O3 -flto -march=native -mtune=native -g; 'make asserts=0' adds -DNDEBUG (README recommends it for maximal performance). Compiler ($(CXX)) and version not stated.
hardware: README: dual Xeon X5675 (2x 6C/12T, 32 GB) and i7-4770 (4C/8T, 16 GB); paper: 2x12-core 2.3 GHz Xeon E5-2670 v3, 512 GB RAM
stars_or_usage: 124 stars; paper by Kerbiriou and Chikhi (copy in repo at paper/paper.pdf)
tradeoffs: Only ASCII text files with bytes in ['\t','~'] work (no binary, no .tar.gz); no CRC32 check (README says adding it would cost about 33%); no multi-member gzip support; standalone program, not a library; output synchronization limits the in-order speedup; needs many cores to win (1 thread: 147 vs 55 MB/s likely reflects its libdeflate-derived inflate code, per the README).
caveats: Prototype: may crash, or give undefined behaviour with asserts=0; blocked/multi-part gzip files and non-ASCII (binary) data are unsupported. pugz skips CRC32 verification while gunzip computes it (README: CRC would cost roughly 33%), so the comparison is not equal work. Paper speeds come from files preloaded in memory with output sent unsynchronized to /dev/null (order-insensitive, mimicking a FASTQ parser); the README 'full decompression' column keeps ordered output and scales far less (251 MB/s at 24 threads vs 1052 MB/s line counting). README speeds are compressed-input bytes per second from a wall-clock shell script (example/bigger_benchmark.sh, divides by 1024*1024) on HIGGS.csv.gz and SRR6832872.fastq.gz. Compiler and version not stated. GitHub fork of ebiggers/libdeflate. The newer rapidgzip (already catalogued) covers the general case.

name: opt_vbyte
baseline: Plain unpartitioned VByte (varint)
workload: Inverted index compressed with VByte vs uniform / eps-optimal / optimal partitioning; space in bits per integer, index build time and query time.
claimed_speedup: README table (i7-4790K): VByte docs 10.498 bpi, freqs 8.031 bpi, build 0.704 s, 4.316 microseconds/query; VByte optimal partitioning docs 7.388 bpi, freqs 4.268 bpi, build 0.739 s, 4.378 microseconds/query. tradeoffs: Partitioning step adds build time and requires sorted lists; decode speed equal to VByte, no speedup.
caveats: Space win, not a speed win: optimal partitioning cuts docs from 10.498 to 7.388 bpi and freqs from 8.031 to 4.268 bpi, while AND-query time is 4.378 vs 4.316 microseconds (about 1.4% slower, derived from page data). baseline: FastPFor (scalar) / varint-G8IU / VByte
workload: Compression and decoding of sorted 32-bit integer lists with differential coding (SIMD-BP128, S4-BP128, SIMD-FastPFOR) plus SIMD intersection of sorted lists.
claimed_speedup: Paper (WebSearch snippets only): SIMD-BP128 nearly twice as fast as the previously fastest schemes (varint-G8IU and PFOR) while saving up to 2 bits per integer; SIMD-BP128-D1-NI 38% faster than SIMD-FastPFOR; S4-BP128-D4 as little as 0.7 CPU cycles per decoded 32-bit integer; SIMD schemes 2-3x faster than FastPFOR and varint with comparable ratio. name: chmike/varint
baseline: Go encoding/binary PutUvarint/Uvarint (LEB128)
workload: Encoding and decoding single unsigned integers of 7 to 63 bits with a big-endian prefix-code varint, ns/op.
claimed_speedup: docs/data.txt (i5-11400, go test -bench): encode at 63 bits 2.992 ns/op versus 5.051 ns/op for binary.PutUvarint (about 1.7x, derived from page data); decode at 63 bits 2.754 versus 5.510 ns/op (about 2.0x, derived from page data); encode+decode round trip at 63 bits 5.726 versus 8.256 ns/op. At 7 bits encode is a tie (0.6907 versus 0.6875 ns/op) and decode is slower than Uvarint (1.154 versus 0.9654 ns/op); the gap opens above 35 bits.
hardware: 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-11400 @ 2.60GHz, Linux amd64 (from docs/data.txt header)
tradeoffs: Different wire format (prefix code, most significant byte first), incompatible with LEB128 and protobuf; the speedup appears mainly for large values. Go only.
caveats: Go version not stated. Win is limited to values over about 35 bits; at 7 bits decode is about 20% slower than the standard library (not inlined), and encode at 14-35 bits is slightly slower. The README itself warns that the benchmark advantages chmike/varint through branch prediction because each run encodes values of a single magnitude. Uses a different wire format (big-endian prefix code), so it is not a drop-in replacement for LEB128 data. Marginal fit for the bitpacking category.

name: dictionary (AVX2/AVX-512 fused bit-unpack plus dictionary decode)
baseline: Scalar binary-unpack-then-lookup dictionary decoder (scalarcodec) in the same repo; not a named external incumbent
workload: Decode 8388608 dictionary-coded 64-bit values (bit-packed indexes into a dictionary of 2 to 1048576 entries) to RAM, measured in cycles per decoded value; the fused AVX2 gather approach unpacks indexes and looks up dictionary values in one step.
claimed_speedup: Skylake, gcc 5.3.0: dictionary size 2 scalarcodec.uncompress 4.00 cycles per value vs AVXDictCODEC::fastuncompress 1.91 (2.1x derived from page data); size 4096 4.14 vs 2.12; size 1048576 11.85 vs 8.47. README: AVX2 decoder 'more than twice as fast as a good scalar decoder' for modest dictionary sizes. Knights Landing, size 2: scalar 7.75 vs AVX2 3.22 vs AVX512DictCODEC 1.48 cycles per value (5.2x derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 5.3.0 (printed in README benchmark output); Makefile sets -fPIC -O3 -march=native -std=c++11 (not stated next to the results)
hardware: Intel Skylake (microarchitecture only, no exact model) and Intel Knights Landing (printed as UNKNOWN)
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 (gather) or AVX-512; dictionary values are hard-coded to 64-bit words; research prototype, not a packaged library. The scalar baseline is the repo's own decoder, not FastPFor, simdcomp or Simple8b.
caveats: Baseline is the authors' own scalar decoder (scalarcodec), not a widely used external incumbent, so baseline_in_list is false. The gain shrinks as the dictionary outgrows cache: Skylake size 65536 scalar 7.14 vs AVX2 fast 5.18 cycles per value, size 1048576 11.85 vs 8.47; the AVX2 path stays faster at every listed size (the earlier note that it was slower at size 8192 was a misreading: size 8192 is 4.35 vs 2.28). README states the code is a demo not meant for production, uses its own format, assumes 64-bit dictionary words, uniform value distribution, and large arrays, and measures steady-state throughput only. 2016 results on gcc 5.3.0, CPU model not exact. Not rerun by anyone independent. The repo now redirects to github.com/fast-pack/dictionary.

name: LeCo (Learn-to-Compress)
baseline: Frame of Reference (FOR), Delta encoding (fixed and variable partitions), Elias-Fano (thirdparty succinct) and rANS, all built inside the repo; Parquet default encoding and RocksDB default index blocks in the system experiments
workload: Lightweight compression of integer columns (fixed-length FOR/Delta/LeCo and variable-length Delta/LeCo variants) measured by compression ratio and random access speed, then integrated into Arrow/Parquet and RocksDB index blocks.
claimed_speedup: Technical report (SIGMOD'24 version): on nine integer data sets LeCo 'achieves a Pareto improvement'; versus FOR and Elias-Fano it improves compression ratio by up to 81% with comparable decompression and random-access speed; versus Delta encoding it is 'an order of magnitude faster in random access' with competitive or better ratio. In Parquet, a filter-scan query runs up to 3.9x faster and bitmap-scan up to 12.6x (up to 5.6x versus FOR); RocksDB throughput rises 16%. Compression throughput (Table 1, GB/s): FOR 0.81, Elias-Fano 0.58, Delta-fix 1.04, Delta-var 0.04, LeCo-fix 0.78, LeCo-var 0.02.
compiler_and_flags: -O3 -march=native, C++17, CMake Release build (CMakeLists.txt); compiler not named (README requires Ubuntu 20.04.4 LTS)
hardware: Intel Xeon (Ice Lake) Platinum 8369B @ 2.70GHz, 32GB DRAM, single thread (microbenchmark); 4x Xeon Platinum 8269CY @ 2.50GHz for the system experiments
tradeoffs: Learned (regression-based) model per segment instead of a fixed frame, so it adds model parameters and training/partitioning cost at encode time. Targets immutable columnar data with random access, not streaming SIMD bit packing.
caveats: No license file in the repo (usability reference). Baselines are FOR, Delta, Elias-Fano and rANS implemented or vendored inside the repo, not FastPFor, simdcomp or Simple8b. The main win is compression ratio at comparable decode speed, plus random-access speed over Delta; LeCo-fix compression throughput is slightly below FOR (0.78 vs 0.81 GB/s) and LeCo-var is about 40x slower to compress than FOR (0.02 GB/s). Numbers come from the technical report that was deleted from the repo on 2023-12-22 (commit 15d679e) and read from history; the published SIGMOD version was not opened (ACM and arXiv blocked). Compiler not named.

name: ledbit/varint (PrefixVarint, leSQLite, leSQLite2 vs LEB128)
baseline: LEB128 varint (as in protobuf and DWARF), implemented in the same repo (leb128.cpp)
workload: Decode time of 100000 log-uniform random integers encoded with each scheme; the repo is a WebAssembly design study (WebAssembly/design issue 601) to pick a faster varint than LEB128.
claimed_speedup: Sample run in README: LEB128 1.165e-03 secs, PrefixVarint 5.693e-04 secs, leSQLite 4.043e-04 secs, leSQLite2 4.815e-04 secs; T(LEB128)/T(PrefixVarint) = 2.047, T(LEB128)/T(leSQLite) = 2.882, T(LEB128)/T(leSQLite2) = 2.420. Size: LEB128 5.076, PrefixVarint 5.060, leSQLite 5.285, leSQLite2 5.239 bytes per integer.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: CXXFLAGS -std=c++14 -O3; compiler not stated
tradeoffs: PrefixVarint keeps the LEB128 size (5.060 vs 5.076 bytes per integer in the sample) but needs unaligned loads and count-trailing-zeros; leSQLite and leSQLite2 are larger (5.285 and 5.239 bytes per integer) and decode faster. Length of an encoded value is known from the first byte.
caveats: README says the C++ code is not production quality and can be driven into undefined behavior by maliciously formed input. Single 100000-integer run, compiler, flags and CPU not stated, so no repeat-run variance and not reproducible as stated. Decode only; encode speed not measured. Not a SIMD or bitpacking library; it is a scalar varint comparison. name: VTEnc
baseline: FastPFor (Delta+FastPFor128/256), Delta+BinaryPacking, Delta+VariableByte, Delta+VarIntGB
workload: Compression ratio and encode/decode speed on sorted lists: ts.txt timestamps and gov2.sorted 32-bit docid lists, Core i7-6700HQ laptop.
claimed_speedup: ts.txt: VTEnc/1 decode 7.32 G/s vs Delta+FastPFor128 3.88 G/s, Delta+FastPFor256 3.61 G/s, Delta+VariableByte 3.43 G/s; ratio 26,622 vs 250.2 for FastPFor128. gov2.sorted: VTEnc/1 ratio 8.29 vs Delta+FastPFor128 6.21, but decode 210.99 M/s vs 615.64 M/s (slower).
tradeoffs: Targets sorted unsigned lists (8/16/32/64-bit); wins on compression ratio and on clustered data like timestamps, loses decode speed on gov2 docids; README warns format may change between versions.
caveats: Speed win holds only on the highly regular timestamp file (ts.txt). On gov2.sorted, VTEnc/1 is slower than every bit-packing and varint baseline but compresses best; only VTEnc/16+ approaches or beats FastPFor decode speed (VTEnc/16 829.11 M/s vs FastPFor256 621.17 M/s, at a slightly lower ratio of 6.10 vs 6.13), and Delta+BinaryPacking/VarIntGB remain faster. Speeds are bytes of uint32 input per second (Google Benchmark SetBytesProcessed), so the ts.txt encode at 102.28 G/s exceeds the laptop's memory bandwidth; VTEnc's bisection over sorted runs with many duplicates evidently skips most input, so this is an algorithmic effect specific to that data, not a general throughput figure (inference from the code, not stated by the author). The encode benchmark does not check output, though the decode benchmark checks equality after decoding. The author runs the shootout; numbers were taken with VTEnc v0.3.0 in 2022. The library is marked as early-stage with no format stability. Last commit 2022-12-01. Tangential to bit-packing, kept because it is compared directly to FastPFor/BinaryPacking/VByte.

Mean of per-query best times (us), PISA vs Lucene 10.4.0 (derived from page data): TOP_10 495 vs 346, TOP_100 641 vs 536, TOP_1000 823 vs 998, TOP_100_COUNT 1586 vs 2737, COUNT 1564 vs 307. The repo README separately cites the ECIR 2019 study: average latency 10-40 ms (top 10) and 20-50 ms (top 1000) on 50M web documents, with no baseline.

name: lexindex
baseline: XCDAT 15 (C++ compressed double-array trie dictionary) and MARISA (marisa-trie 0.2.6)
workload: Compressed string dictionary (string to dense id and back) over 13 corpora (Wikipedia titles, domains, PyPI names, paths, identifiers, UUIDs, DNA and others) at 1M and 10M keys; measures serialized bytes per key, single-key lookup latency, build time.
claimed_speedup: Smallest structure on 13 of 13 corpora at 1M keys against the campaign's MARISA and XCDAT builds (e.g. words 2.51 vs 2.98 B/key for MARISA rho=2; titles-en 7.21 vs 8.19). HashedDictIndex (closed) lookup 14 to 61 ns against XCDAT 15's 54 to 449 ns at 1M keys. Strict exact-search structures still trail XCDAT 15 on 9 of 13 corpora at 1M keys.
compiler_and_flags: C++ competitors (MARISA, XCDAT driver) built with c++ -O3 -march=native -std=c++17 (-DNDEBUG for XCDAT and floor drivers) per harness/build.sh; GCC 16.2.1, rustc 1.98.1; lexindex 4.5.2 from crates.io
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800HS (8 cores / 16 threads), Fedora 44, measured 2026-09-26
tradeoffs: Immutable string-to-id indexes only. Seven index types trade size against speed: front-coded DictIndex is smallest but slowest to look up; HashedDictIndex adds a perfect hash for fast id lookup. Rust crate with Python bindings and a C ABI, so usable from C++ only through the C interface.
caveats: Harness author is the lexindex author (conflict of interest, disclosed in the README; harness pins every competitor, fetches lexindex 4.5.2 from crates.io and publishes JSON artifacts). The 14 to 61 ns closed HashedDictIndex lookup returns some id for keys that were never inserted, so it is not equivalent to the tries' exact search. lexindex's fastest exact search trails XCDAT 15 on 9 of 13 corpora at 1M keys (5 percent on uuid to 57 percent on pypi), wins dna (0.95x) and numeric (0.55x); at 10M keys it wins dna, numeric, urls and titles-en and loses opaque (1.36x). Against MARISA at its smallest (1 to 32 tries, tiny cache, untimed) the size margin shrinks to 0.04 percent on paths and 3.8 percent on titles-en at 1M, 0.11 to 0.30 percent on titles-en/urls at 10M, and MARISA is smaller once loaded (mmap) on five rows. The numeric corpus win (301 bytes total) is a degenerate dense-id case. Baselines are succinct tries (MARISA, XCDAT, CoCo-trie, PDT, FST, C2 variants), not SDSL or sux directly. String-index-benchmarks repo has 0 stars.

name: sucds
baseline: vers-vecs RsVec and succinctly BitVec (Rust crates), not SDSL

name: wavelet_forest
baseline: SDSL Huffman-shaped wavelet tree (sdsl-lite), uncompressed bitvectors
workload: access queries (10,000 random positions) on synthetic multi-GB texts over bit, base-4, octal, hex and ASCII alphabets; wavelet forest built with fixed block sizes from 50 KB to 10 MB versus one global wavelet tree.
claimed_speedup: README, no numbers: wavelet forest 'often outperforms' the wavelet tree on larger alphabets (ASCII); faster for hex across a broad range of block sizes; blocks of about 0.5 MB frequently best; speedups are not monotonic in block size.
compiler_and_flags: C++17 via CMake (CMakeLists.txt sets no build type or optimization flags; OpenMP if found). The README says g++ >= 12 with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release.
tradeoffs: Gain comes from cache locality of per-block trees; the README tests uncompressed bitvectors only, so space behavior with compressed bitvectors is not shown. Per-block alphabets and metadata add overhead. Targets access, with rank 'often'.
caveats: No numbers in the repo; the claim rests on the SPIRE 2024 paper 'Another Virtue of Wavelet Forests' (arXiv 2308.07809), which was not opened. The README describes a benchmark harness (gen_text, build_wt, build_wf, bench_access, CSV output, a block-size sweep) that does not exist in the repo. The actual timing code, src/main.cpp, has hard-coded placeholder file paths and a fixed 10 MB block; its wavelet-tree loop discards the result of wt[i] (the compiler may remove it), while the forest loop prints every character to stdout inside the timed region, so the two timings are not comparable. The README calls the license permissive, but the LICENSE file is GPL-3.0 and the source headers say 'Copyright (c) Boucher Lab. All rights reserved. Licensed under the GNU license'. Research-grade code, 1 star.

name: 3star-rankselect (3* rank/select)
baseline: SDSL (sd_vector, mcl select), sux (rank9sel, simple_select), pasta flat rank/select, Poppy (benchmark script options)
workload: Rank and select on plain bit vectors with worst-case constant query time; repo script benchmarks select_1 query time (ns) and space overhead percent against competitor code it downloads.
claimed_speedup: Space: paper abstract (search snippet) reports 0.78 percent overhead, 4.5x to 64.1x less than previous implementations. Checked-in logs (1e9 bits, density 0.5, 2e7 random select_1 queries, i9-13900H): m3 overhead 0.82 percent vs simple_s1 2.34, pasta flat 3.58, simple_s3 7.03, sdsl_mcl 23.63, rank9sel 56.25, sdsl_sd 78.15 percent (2.9x to 95x less overhead, derived from page data). Query time is not a win: m3 100.4 ns vs simple_s1 100.2, rank9sel 100.3, sdsl_mcl 80.9, simple_s3 49.1 ns in the same run; a second run gives m3 95 to 96 ns (0.82 percent config) or 77 to 79 ns (3.2 percent config) vs 76 to 185 ns for competitors depending on density.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 18.1.3, -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG (CMakeLists.txt and log RESULT lines)
hardware: 13th Gen Intel Core i9-13900H (from checked-in log lines)
tradeoffs: Targets minimal space overhead with worst-case constant-time queries; the README does not claim faster queries than pasta or SDSL, only 'good practical performance'.
caveats: Paper (arXiv 2509.17819, Kurpicz, Rigi-Luperti, Sanders) is blocked here; its 4.5x to 64.1x figure comes from a search snippet. The checked-in logs are single-instance, single-iteration example runs (the README calls the script an exemplary benchmark) and include one run tagged 'vb', apparently a virtual machine. The claim is about space overhead; at the 0.82 percent setting select_1 is level with rank9sel and simple_select s1 and about 2x slower than simple_select s3 and slower than SDSL mcl. Reproduction script clones competitor repos (sdsl-lite, sux, rankselect, rankselect2) at their heads, not pinned commits.

baseline: MARISA (marisa-trie), FST (SuRF), CoCo-trie

Independent rerun at 1M keys on 12 corpora (string-index-benchmarks artifact, derived from page data, rho=0 vs rho=0 lookup latency): C2-MARISA 1.21x to 1.48x faster than MARISA on all 12; C2-FST 1.05x to 1.82x faster than FST on 11 and 0.87x (slower) on opaque; C2-CoCo against the original CoCo-trie is slower on 7 of 8 corpora where both ran (0.78x to 0.92x) and faster only on urls (1.49x). name: Darts-clone
baseline: Darts (Double-ARray Trie System, original header library by Taku Kudo)
workload: Static double-array trie dictionaries built from 7 key sets (Japanese and English word lists, Wikipedia titles, Google unigram lists, 7-digit postal codes; 118k to 13.6M keys); average ns per key for exactMatchSearch(), commonPrefixSearch() and traverse(), keys queried in lexicographic and in random order, plus dictionary size and build time.
claimed_speedup: Random-order exactMatchSearch: JA1 170.4 vs 76.2 ns/key (about 2.2x faster, derived from page data), EN1 228.5 vs 111.3 ns/key (about 2.1x, derived from page data), EN3 545.3 vs 453.3 ns/key. Lexicographic exactMatchSearch: JA1 48.9 vs 33.1 ns/key. Dictionary size about halved (JA1 7,023 KB vs 3,336 KB; EN2 513,873 KB vs 240,634 KB). Build time lower when no values are given (JA1 828 vs 368 ns/key), but higher when every key has a unique value (JA1 1,196 ns/key, EN2 6,666 vs 2,518 ns/key).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.3.3 (optimization flags not stated on the page); benchmark tool darts-benchmark ships with the repo
hardware: Dell Precision T3400, Core 2 Quad Q9550 2.83GHz, 64-bit Ubuntu 9.04
stars_or_usage: 161 stars; packaged as a vcpkg port (darts-clone)
tradeoffs: Static dictionary (no updates). Not a true succinct structure: it is a compact double-array trie (32-bit units, DAWG-merged), so it is far larger than LOUDS or MARISA tries (marisa-trie README lists 376,613,888 bytes for darts-clone against 50,753,560 for marisa-trie on 9.8M Wikipedia titles). Build time grows when every key has a unique value (JA2 5,942 ns/key). Dictionary files are not compatible with Darts.
caveats: Baseline is the original Darts, not SDSL or sux. Numbers are from a 2009-2011 era machine and compiler (gcc 4.3.3, Darts-clone 0.32g), on a Japanese-language page; optimization flags are not stated. Results are mixed: on the postal-code set (DIG) Darts-clone is slower for exactMatchSearch (24.2 vs 18.8 ns/key lexicographic, 43.9 vs 40.2 random), and lexicographic traverse() is slower on every word list (for example JA2 144.6 vs 119.1 ns/key); the page attributes this to traverse() not being inlined. Build time is lower only when no values are associated; with unique values per key, build is slower than Darts on every corpus (for example EN2 6,666 vs 2,518 ns/key). The page itself warns that search time depends heavily on cache sizes, inlining and key distribution. On the large Wikipedia and n-gram sets the random-order gain is smaller (JA2 516.4 vs 620.8 ns/key). Found as a registry hit, but it is a compact trie rather than a rank/select structure, so category fit is loose. Recent commits (May 2025) are documentation edits; the author does not state the project is finished.

name: rankselect (PTSelect, splatlab)
baseline: SDSL rank/select support (also CS-Poppy)
workload: Rank and select queries on uncompressed bit vectors, plus select on single 64-bit words using PDEP and TZCNT (PTSelect); the repo has bitmap_bench.cc and bitmap_bench_sdsl.cc that time the same queries on this code and on SDSL.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (arXiv 1706.00990, not opened): PTSelect, a 4-instruction machine-word select (PDEP + TZCNT), is 2x-4x faster than the previous state-of-the-art 64-bit word select; select on bit vectors is 2.2x-6x faster than CS-Poppy and SDSL.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: g++ -std=c++11 -O9 -mpopcnt -msse4 -I. -Iinclude/ -Iinclude/sdsl
tradeoffs: Select via PDEP needs a Haswell-or-later x86 CPU (BMI2). Rank/select over uncompressed bit sequences only. Bundles an old copy of SDSL headers for the comparison.
caveats: Speedup numbers come only from search snippets of arXiv preprint 1706.00990 (arXiv and a third-party summary blog are blocked here). The README is one line with no numbers, and no CPU model appears in the repo. The repo is a GitHub fork of efficient/rankselect (CMU's CS-Poppy code, Apache-2.0, copyright 2013 CMU); this fork adds PTSelect (select64_pdep_tzcnt in popcount.h, used by select64) and the SDSL benchmark. It needs a Haswell-or-later CPU with BMI2, although the Makefile passes only -mpopcnt -msse4 because PDEP/TZCNT come in through inline asm. Timing uses gettimeofday. It bundles an older SDSL version (2017). Newer work (pasta bit_vector, sux) is already catalogued and likely faster. Preprint; peer-review status not verified.

name: vers (vers-vecs)

name: AWRY
baseline: AvxWindowFmIndex (C), SeqAn3 FM-index, SDSL
workload: None in this repo: the README has no benchmark. The C original (AvxWindowFmIndex) paper snippet claims 2-4x faster nucleotide exact-match queries than SeqAn3.
claimed_speedup: None for AWRY. README calls it 'fastest in its class' by reference to the C library paper (doi 10.1186/s13015-021-00204-6); search snippet: C version 2-4x faster than SeqAn3 on nucleotides, 2-6x on amino acids (snippet only).
